m: Om. I bow to the Goddess seated on a lotus, her lustre like a thousand rising suns, dressed in red silk, wearing a garland on her head, her breasts coloured with red, holding in her lotus hands a rosary, knowledge, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon, the beauty of her lotus face shining with three eyes,
her crown bound with the jewel of the cool-rayed moon. Om. The seer said:
Seeing that army being slaughtered, the great asura Chikshura, the general, grew angry and went to fight Ambika.
That asura rained a shower of arrows on the Goddess in battle, as a cloud rains a shower of water on a peak of Mount Meru.
The Goddess then cut his masses of arrows as if in play, and with her arrows she struck his horses and the driver of those horses.
She at once cut his bow and his banner, raised very high, and she pierced the one whose bow was cut, in his limbs, with swift arrows.
His bow cut, his chariot gone, his horses slain, his charioteer slain, the asura rushed at the Goddess bearing sword and shield.
Striking the lion on the head with a sharp-edged sword, he also, with great speed, struck the Goddess on the left arm.
His sword, O joy of kings, on reaching her arm, broke. Then, his eyes red, he seized a spear in anger.
The great asura then hurled it at Bhadrakali, blazing with splendour like the orb of the sun from the sky.
Seeing that spear coming, the Goddess released her own spear. By it that spear was broken into a hundred pieces, and so was that great asura.
When that general of Mahisha's army, of great valour, was slain, Chamara, tormentor of the gods, came mounted on an elephant.
He too released a spear at the Goddess. Ambika quickly struck it down with a humkara and made it fall to the earth, its light gone.
Seeing the spear broken and fallen, Chamara, filled with anger, hurled a trident, and she cut that too with arrows.
Then the lion leapt up, stood between the elephant's frontal lobes, and fought that enemy of the gods high up, in a battle of arms.
Fighting, the two of them then came down from that elephant to the earth, and, exceedingly enraged, they fought with very dreadful blows.
Then the enemy of beasts leapt swiftly into the sky, fell, and with a blow of his paw severed Chamara's head.
Udagra was slain by the Goddess in battle with rocks, trees, and the like, and Karala was struck down with teeth, fists, and palms.
The angry Goddess crushed the arrogant one with blows of the mace. With a bhindipala she slew Bashkala, and with arrows Tamra and Andhaka.
The three-eyed supreme sovereign also slew with her trident Ugrasya of fierce valour, and likewise Mahahanu.
With her sword she made Bidala's head fall from his body, and with arrows she sent both Durdhara and Durmukha to Yama's abode.
As his own army was thus being destroyed, Mahishasura, in his buffalo form, terrified those hosts.
Some he struck with his snout, others with kicks of his hooves, others he beat with his tail, and others he tore with his two horns.
Others he felled to the ground by his speed, by his roar, by his wheeling about, and others by the wind of his breath.
Having felled the front of the army, that asura rushed to kill the lion of the great Goddess. Then Ambika became angry.
He too, of great valour, in anger, the earth torn by his hooves, hurled high mountains with his two horns, and he roared.
The earth, torn by the wheeling of his speed, broke apart. Struck by his tail, the ocean flooded on every side.
Clouds, split by his shaken horns, fell to pieces. Mountains, by the hundred, fell from the sky at the winds of his breath.
Seeing that great asura rushing on, swollen with anger, Chandika then became angry for the sake of slaying him.
She threw her noose over him and bound that great asura. Bound in that great fight, he too abandoned his buffalo form.
Then he at once became a lion. While Ambika was cutting off his head, he appeared as a man with a sword in his hand.
At once the Goddess cut that man with her arrows, together with his sword and shield. Then he became a great elephant.
With his trunk he dragged the great lion, and he roared. As he dragged, the Goddess cut off his trunk with her sword.
Then the great asura again took a buffalo body, and in the same way he threw the three worlds, with what moves and what does not move, into turmoil.
Then the angry Mother of the world, Chandika, drank the excellent drink, again and again, and she laughed, her eyes red.
That asura too roared, puffed up with the pride of strength and valour, and with his two horns he hurled mountains at Chandika.
She, pulverizing with masses of arrows those mountains he had thrown, spoke to him, whose face was flushed and whose speech was confused by intoxication.
The Goddess said:
Roar, roar for a moment, fool, while I drink this wine. When you have been slain by me, the gods will soon roar here.
The seer said:
Having spoken thus, she leapt up, mounted that great asura, pressed his neck with her foot, and struck him with her spear.
Then he, pressed by her foot, came halfway out of his own mouth, caught by the Goddess's valour.
That great asura, only halfway out and still fighting, was felled when the Goddess cut off his head with her great sword.
Then the whole daitya army cried out in woe and perished. All the hosts of gods attained the highest joy.
The gods praised that Goddess, together with the divine great seers. The lords of the gandharvas sang, and the bands of apsarases danced.
